posts.title: Spiritual Living and the Krotona Institute of Theosophy
posts.description: Ananya Sri Ram speaks with George Alger about the Krotona Institute of Theosophy to discuss the history, philosophy, and daily life of Ojai’s oldest spiritual community. What is Theosophy? Sri Ram explains that the word theosophy stems from the ancient Greek theosophia, tracing back to the 3rd-century Alexandrian Neoplatonists, and was later modernized in the late 19th century by Helena Blavatsky, co-founder of the Theosophical Society. At its core, theosophy is the study of “divine wisdom” and the fundamental oneness of all life. Blavatsky played a pivotal role in introducing Eastern spiritual teachings to the West, weaving together foundational concepts from Buddhism and Hinduism alongside elements of Kabbalah and other traditions. An Intentional Community Rooted in Ancient Tradition Founded in Hollywood in 1920 before relocating to Ojai in 1924, the Krotona Institute is celebrating over a century of spiritual study. posts.title: 5x5x5: Performance Art, Chaos, and Community
posts.description: Steve Aguilar speaks with Our Ventura TV host MB Hanrahan about the 5x5x5 performance series. Aguilar shares his multidisciplinary background across music, writing, philosophy, photography, filmmaking, production, and performance, and discusses how he took over the series after the passing of its founder, renowned performance artist and painter John White. Origins and Evolution of 5x5x5 : Aguilar traces the series back roughly two decades to John White—whose work has been shown at institutions like the Guggenheim and the Getty and featured in Pacific Standard Time—and his connection to Ventura’s organic Art City artist community. He recalls the show moving between spaces such as the Sylvia White Gallery on Main Street and Namba Arts, before expanding beyond its original five-minute performance art format to include musicians, poets, and storytellers while keeping performance art at its core. posts.title: Wild Patients Don’t Have Health Insurance: Santa Barbara Wildlife Care Network
posts.description: Becky Gaal and Pam Perrimon from the Santa Barbara Wildlife Care Network (SBWCN) speak with George Alger about their mission, operations, and community involvement across Santa Barbara and Ventura counties. Mission & Patients : SBWCN rescues, rehabilitates, and releases orphaned, oiled, and injured wildlife. They have treated over 5,250 animals across 210 species, with their most common patients including mallards, Virginia opossums, pigeons, and crows. Intake fluctuates seasonally, shifting from orphaned baby animals in the spring to emaciated and dehydrated seabirds later in the year. What to Do When Finding Injured Wildlife : If residents encounter a distressed animal, they are advised to observe the species from a safe distance and call SBWCN’s helpline rather than immediately intervening.
